nameStory: Scarlet flax gets its striking name from its brilliant red flowers that practically glow in the garden. The word 'flax' comes from the Old English 'fleax,' referring to the plant fibers that have been used to make linen for thousands of years. While this ornamental cousin isn't typically used for fiber, it shares the same sleek, narrow leaves and delicate branching structure as its more utilitarian relatives.
description: Scarlet flax is a slender annual flower that stands about 1-2 feet tall with an upright, branching stem. Its most striking feature is its vibrant red, five-petaled flowers that can reach over an inch across, creating brilliant splashes of color in gardens and naturalized areas. The plant has narrow, waxy lance-shaped leaves that feel smooth and somewhat thick to the touch. Originally from North Africa, this eye-catching plant occasionally escapes cultivation in New England but rarely survives our winters.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five brilliant red petals that feel silky and delicate, each up to an inch long, with stamens topped by anthers carrying distinctive pale blue pollen that contrasts beautifully with the red petals

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves about half an inch to an inch long that feel waxy and smooth, arranged alternately along the branching stems

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, upright annual that branches gracefully, typically 1-2 feet tall with a delicate, airy appearance despite its sturdy stems

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, somewhat waxy stems that branch repeatedly, feeling firm but not woody, with flowers held on individual stalks several inches long

habitat: In New England, scarlet flax is most commonly found as an escape from gardens, appearing along roadsides, in disturbed soils, and occasionally in old garden sites. It prefers well-drained, sunny locations and can tolerate poor soils. Since it's not winter-hardy here, any wild populations are temporary and depend on recent seed dispersal from cultivated plants.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms, producing small rosettes of narrow leaves that are easily overlooked.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with brilliant red flowers opening throughout the warm months, most spectacular in July and August.
seasonality.fall: Late-season flowers may continue into early fall, followed by small seed capsules that split open to release seeds before frost.
seasonality.winter: Plants die completely with first hard frost, leaving no above-ground trace - only seeds remain to potentially germinate the following year.

funFact: The stamens of scarlet flax produce pale blue pollen that creates a stunning color contrast with the bright red petals - it's like nature's own patriotic color scheme! This blue pollen is so distinctive that you can often spot it dusting the petals and visiting insects.
confusionNotes: The brilliant red color and five-petaled flowers make scarlet flax fairly distinctive, but it might be confused with red poppies. Remember that poppies have papery, crinkled petals and milky sap, while flax has smooth, silky petals and clear sap.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'flax,' scarlet flax is grown purely for ornament and isn't used to make linen like its famous cousin, common flax. Many gardeners grow it as an easy annual, but be aware that in some areas it can self-seed enthusiastically - though in New England's climate, it rarely persists without human help.
compareHints: Among New England's flax species, scarlet flax is the only one with bright red flowers - all our native flaxes have yellow, blue, or white blooms. Its flowers are also notably larger than most of its relatives, and unlike perennial flax which has blue flowers and comes back each year, scarlet flax is an annual with unmistakable red blooms.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sandplain Flax differs from other New England flax species primarily by its habitat preference for sandy soils and coastal areas.

Ridged Yellow Flax stands out from its New England flax relatives primarily by those distinctive stem ridges - Stiff Yellow Flax has smooth stems and grows more upright, while Virginia Flax has smooth stems and much smaller white or pale yellow flowers.

Common flax stands out from its wild New England relatives by being much taller and more robust than species like Fairy Flax, and having blue flowers instead of the yellow blooms found on Ridged Yellow Flax or Stiff Yellow Flax.

Virginia Flax is distinguished from other wild flaxes in New England by its yellow flowers and branching habit - Fairy Flax has white flowers, while the yellow-flowered Ridged Yellow Flax has more linear leaves and grows in different habitats.
Fairy flax stands out from other New England flax species by being much smaller and more delicate than its relatives.
Perennial flax stands out from other New England flax species by its perennial nature and pure blue flowers.
Among the yellow-flowered flax species in eastern North America, Stiff Yellow Flax stands out for its notably rigid stems that won't bend easily.
